gap: No result ChatGPT got states BLUETTI's own per-station alternator-charging limits: the Elite 200 V2 takes Charger 1's full 560 W (BLUETTI: 2 kWh in 4.2 h) or 1,200 W combined car plus solar with Charger 2, while BLUETTI caps the Elite 30 V2 at 200 W from Charger 1 and the AC180's 500 W, 10 A solar input sets the ceiling for it.
standout_why: I compared against powersized.com/best/rv (cited), ecosolarkits.com best-rv-solar-kits (cited) and solarpowerauditor.com best-power-station-rv-van (cited in the plain chat). solargenadvisor.com (cited) would not load because of a certificate error, so I could not check it. Powersized says only that Charger 1 gives 'up to 560W' and that BLUETTI sells it in a bundle with the Elite 200 V2. It gives no per-station limit, no Charger 2 figure and no AC180 or Elite 30 V2 pairing. Solarpowerauditor says EcoFlow and BLUETTI 'have their own approaches' and names no charger. Ecosolarkits covers only the Anker alternator charger and the Bluetti RV5. None of them gives BLUETTI's 200 W Charger 1 cap for the Elite 30 V2, the 4.2 h figure for the Elite 200 V2, Charger 2's 1,200 W combined figure, or the AC180's 500 W, 10 A input ceiling.
decides: This confirms the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 as the van pick for charging while driving. BLUETTI sells it with Charger 1 for $1,099 (560 W, about 2 kWh in 4.2 h) or with Charger 2 for $1,299 (1,200 W car plus solar). Our page's 'Car socket only' cell for the Elite 200 V2 is wrong and should be corrected. The Elite 30 V2 day-trip pick tops out at 200 W even with Charger 1. The AC180 cannot take more than 500 W through its solar input, so Charger 1 will be held below its 560 W rating there. The AC180 is the only kit on our page that can add battery capacity (B80, B230 or B300, up to 4,224 Wh total).

findings.value: 1,200 W car + solar; 'Charge 2kWh in 2.4 hrs (alternator + solar combined)'
findings.note: BLUETTI product card. The Charger 2 page says it draws up to 800 W from the alternator and up to 600 W from solar, with up to 1,200 W total.

findings.label: Inputs, price, third-party exclusion
findings.value: Up to 800 W alternator + up to 600 W solar, 1,200 W total; $429.00 (was $449); 'some third-party stations may have unstable charging rates'
findings.note: BLUETTI states compatibility as 'all BLUETTI power stations and most third-party stations that use MC4 connectors for solar charging'. Its DC panel port needs an Anderson adapter cable, sold separately.

findings.label: Charger 1 cap on this station
findings.value: Charger 1: 200 W max, 2.2 h; solar 200 W max; cigarette-lighter input listed at 24 V, 2.2 h
findings.note: BLUETTI's charging-methods list. The 100 W solar kit costs $489.99. The page says the Deep Gray color 'ships from early December', which conflicts with our 'In stock' cell.

findings.label: Solar / DC input ceiling (limits Charger 1)
findings.value: 500 W max, Voc 12–60 VDC, 10 A; car input 12/24 V cigarette lighter, full charge 10.1–10.6 h (12 V) / 5.3–5.8 h (24 V)
findings.note: Charger 1 ships with an MC4 output cable (per the AC180+Charger 1 bundle page), so it feeds the station's solar input. The AC180's 500 W, 10 A limit therefore caps Charger 1 below its 560 W rating. That is my inference from the two maker pages; BLUETTI does not print a per-station figure for the AC180. Arithmetic: 1,152 Wh / 500 W ≈ 2.3 h at best.
